t: LeetCode 1621 — Number of Sets of K Non-Overlapping Line Segments
o: Points sit at x = 0 .. n-1 on a line; a segment picks two points and covers the interval between them. Exactly k pairwise non-overlapping segments must be drawn, with shared endpoints allowed. Example 1 (n = 4, k = 2) has five arrangements such as {(0,2), (2,3)}. Thinking in the n-1 unit gaps between adjacent points turns geometry into combinatorics: each segment occupies a contiguous run of gaps, and non-overlap means the chosen runs are pairwise disjoint (touching runs correspond to a shared endpoint). A state-machine DP over the points and a closed-form binomial C(n+k-1, 2k) both solve it; answers are taken modulo 10^9 + 7 because counts explode quickly.
k: Map each segment to a non-empty contiguous run of the n-1 gaps; non-overlapping segments are exactly disjoint gap runs.
A point-by-point DP with an "open segment" flag handles shared endpoints elegantly: a new segment may start on the same point where another just closed.
Stars and bars gives the closed form C(n+k-1, 2k), enabling an O(n+k) solution via factorials mod 10^9+7.

a.n: Approach 1: Point-by-Point DP with Open/Closed States
a.i: Sweep points left to right keeping dp[j][0] = ways with j finished segments and no active segment, and dp[j][1] = ways with j finished segments plus one open segment currently extending. At each new point you may skip it, extend the open segment, close it here, or open a new one — crucially, opening may follow a closing at the same point, which is precisely how shared endpoints arise. Rolling arrays keep memory at O(k).
s: Initialize dp[0][0] = 1 (empty configuration before any point).
For each of the n points sweep j from k down to 1: dp[j][0] += dp[j-1][1] (close an open segment here), then dp[j][1] += dp[j][0] (extend, or open after closing at this same point).
Handle j = 0 separately: dp[0][1] += dp[0][0] (open the first segment).
a.t: O(n·k) — two constant-time transitions per (point, segment-count) pair.

a.i: Shrink each chosen gap-run by deleting one gap (runs are non-empty) and treat the k runs as separated by k inserted separators; a classical bijection then counts disjoint non-empty consecutive runs among m = n-1 gaps as C(m + k, 2k) = C(n+k-1, 2k). Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 10^9+7 — using Fermat's little theorem for inverses since the modulus is prime — and evaluate the binomial in O(1).
s: Build factorial table fact[0..m] mod p.
Build inverse factorials: invFact[m] = fact[m]^(p-2) mod p, then descend.
Return fact[m] * invFact[2k] * invFact[m - 2k] mod p.
a.t: O(n + k) — building the factorial tables dominates; the binomial itself is O(1) plus a modular exponentiation.

w:
## Wrap-up

Default to the DP in an interview — it is easier to defend and generalizes naturally (weighted segments, forbidden gaps); quote the binomial as a bonus insight. **Pitfalls:** forgetting that shared endpoints are legal — transitions must permit close-then-open on the same point; applying the modulus too late and overflowing 32-bit intermediates in C++/Java (use 64-bit math); off-by-one in the formula — sanity-check against n=3,k=1 → 3 and n=4,k=2 → 5.

**Edge cases:** k = 1 reduces to n(n-1)/2 segments... verify against C(n, 2); k up to n-1 always admits at least the all-adjacent-pairs tiling. **Follow-ups:** count configurations covering every point, maximize total covered length, or handle forbidden intervals.
